errors.statement: A highest education of 1st-4th grade lowers the predicted chance to about 10% and 7th-8th grade to about 19% (across the whole model / through this sum alone)
errors.check: probe --hold typical --set education=3 --sweep education-num=2,10: 89.8% / 9.9%; education=5 with education-num 4,10: 86.5% / 19.3%. subgroup education=='3' and education-num==10: n=0; education=='3': n=189, mean predicted 95.1%, observed 96.3%. The numbers reproduce as one-at-a-time counterfactuals, which the text says they are. But the combination is off-support, and a real person with that schooling gets a higher chance, so the sentence misleads. It is not wrong under the stated counterfactual reading.
errors.reconcile_note: K1 kept weakened: the sentences change one input for the typical person ('Changing one input at a time ...', '... lowers it to about 10%') and do not make a claim about real people with that schooling.

errors.statement: Higher capital gains lower the predicted chance slowly at first, then faster
errors.check: probe --hold typical --sweep capital-gain=0:7000:8: 61.9, 52.9, 43.6, 34.8, 26.9, 20.2, 11.5, 5.7% (drops of 9.0, 9.3, 8.8, 7.9, 6.7, 8.7, 5.8 points per $1000), so the chance has no slow start. The claim's 'accelerating' shape is on the log-odds scale (slope -0.00037 then -0.00076 per $, kink ~$5258), where it is right. A log-odds shape is written as a shape of the chance.

subgroup capital-gain == 0: n=35788 of 39073 = 91.6%, not 95%. capital-gain < 5246 (below the kink): 95.5%, so the 95% is the below-kink share attached to the cg=0 value. The +0.406 contribution reproduces, but the share does not reproduce for the population named.
